Francisco Lindor and Manny Machado continue to be two of the highest-paid infielders in Major League Baseball, both signed to nine-figure, long-term contracts. Lindor’s deal with the New York Mets extends through 2031, while Machado’s extension with the San Diego Padres extends through 2033.
The financial comparison is more than headline contract values. Their net worth includes their 2026 salary and all career earnings in MLB, as well as endorsements, investments and real estate holdings. However, specific personal net worth figures are not publicly available and are subject to estimation, not official disclosure.
Francisco Lindor and Manny Machado net worth comparison in 2026
Francisco Lindor and Manny Machado are also in the same ballpark of wealth, according to public estimates, in 2026. Lindor’s deal with the Mets has greatly boosted his wealth, while Machado has built up big earnings thanks to his contracts with the Padres and his previous MLB deals.
Celebrity Net Worth reports that Lindor’s current deal is for $341 million over 10 years, and it keeps him signed through the 2031 season. The deal Machado signed is bigger in total value at $350 million over 11 years and runs through 2033, according to Celebrity Net Worth.

| Estimated net worth | $75M–$100M | $75M–$100M |
| Current MLB team | New York Mets | San Diego Padres |
| Current contract | 10 years, $341M | 11 years, $350M |
| Contract through | 2031 | 2033 |
| 2026 total salary/payroll figure | $32.48M | $25.09M |

Lindor’s financial foundation is a 10-year, $341 million deal with the Mets. Celebrity Net Worth said the deal averages $34.1 million a year and was designed to keep the All-Star shortstop in New York through the 2031 season.
According to Celebrity Net Worth, Lindor is ranked as one of the highest-paid players in Major League Baseball in 2026 with a total compensation of approximately $32.48 million. Career earnings projections have also climbed above $200 million, a nod to his time with Cleveland and New York.
Manny Machado wealth profile with San Diego Padres
Machado’s wealth comes from an elite MLB career and successive blockbuster contracts. Per Celebrity Net Worth, the Padres finalised his 11-year, $350 million extension in February 2023, keeping him in San Diego through the 2033 season.
The average annual value of the contract is approximately $31.82 million. His reported 2026 salary is about $25.09 million, according to Celebrity Net Worth. But the contract structure boosts his salary in later seasons, with Baseball-Reference listing an average of $39.1 million per year from 2027 to 2033.
Machado’s financial portfolio is not just his playing salary. His long career in the MLB, along with endorsements and property holdings, has helped establish other sources of wealth, although specific private investments and asset values are not fully disclosed.
Lindor and Machado contract earnings compared in 2026
The headline numbers give you a sense of how close the two financial profiles are, but they also reveal an important difference in the structure of the contract. Machado has the larger overall commitment at $350 million, according to Celebrity Net Worth, but Lindor has the larger average annual value at $34.1 million.
Lindor is also making more in 2026 than Machado is reportedly making. Celebrity Net Worth has Lindor’s AP-derived salary data at about $32.48 million for the season and Machado’s at $25.09 million.

| Total current contract | $341M | $350M |
| Contract length | 10 years | 11 years |
| Average annual value | $34.1M | $31.82M |
| 2026 compensation | $32.48M | $25.09M |
| Contract expiration | 2031 | 2033 |
| Major MLB position | Shortstop | Third baseman |
That means the two are still among the highest-paid players in baseball. Lindor’s deal has the higher average salary, while Machado’s contract has the higher guaranteed amount and that extra year of contractual security. Their future net worths will also depend on taxes, spending, investment performance, endorsements and the value of assets accumulated from their careers.

item.content:encoded:
Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor understands how momentous Saturday at Citi Field is.
The organization is honoring Carlos Beltrán by inducting him into the Mets Hall of Fame and retiring his No. 15. Beltrán is a player who not only represented the franchise as one of its best players, but as a fellow Puerto Rican, the honor hits close to home for Lindor.
"It's very inspiring. Someone that was close to me and to every Puerto Rican. Anybody that's Puerto Rican that makes it big, us Puerto Ricans feel like we made it as well," Lindor said in the clubhouse prior to Saturday's game. "To be on the biggest stages, playoffs, All-Star games and to see him come back to the island is very special. We always talk about guys like that, like the Beltráns, [Roberto] Alomar, [Carlos] Delgado, [Ivan]Rodriguez. Guys that set the path for a guy like me today."
Lindor looked up to Beltrán because he was also a switch-hitter from the island, who played hard and "had swag," but he wouldn't get a chance to build a relationship with one of his idols until 2016.
Lindor, playing with Cleveland at the time, just wrapped up a series with the Beltrán's Yankees right before the All-Star break. The young shortstop was heading to San Diego for his first All-Star Game and shared a plane with the outfielder and a few other Yankees who also made the Midsummer Classic. That's when he had an opportunity to speak with the future Hall of Famer.
"Anybody that's from Puerto Rico and makes it big, us Puerto Ricans feel like we made it, as well."
Francisco Lindor says it was "very inspiring" to see Carlos Beltrán's success in Major League Baseball: pic.twitter.com/5QX8pUuM4n
"He's a mentor. Someone you can have a conversation with him, tell him the stuff I'm going through because he probably already went through it. He's helped me for sure," Lindor said of Beltrán. "I look up to him growing up and to have an opportunity to share the field with him. To have moments to talk to him. It's something I don't take for granted."
That relationship came in handy when Lindor was traded to the Mets in 2021. It was an adjustment period for Lindor, who struggled on and off the field. Going from a small market to New York City was tough for Lindor, but he had Beltrán to help him.
Beltran got Lindor in touch with a realtor and helped him with the off-the-field transition, but also offered a shoulder when the on-the-field production wasn't there.
"When I first got traded here, I called him and I talked to him," Lindor said. "I didn't play well. I sucked in the beginning and having him there to comfort me and say, 'Hey, this stuff is going to happen. It's ok. You're going to go through stuff like this, but you're going to come out on the other side. Stay true to yourself and play the game the right way.'
"Stuff like that early on was huge for me today."
Five years later, and Lindor has become an important part of the team on the field and as a locker room leader.
"I love Francisco. I admire him. I love the way he plays. I always watch the switch-hitters in the game," Beltrán said prior to his number retirement ceremony. "He will be in this position at some point in life. I'm grateful for the friendship that we have...We have a good relationship. We talk about baseball, we talk about hitting, life, family, we talk about kids, we talk about everything.
"The relationship I was able to build with him is a friendship more than anything else."
Could that relationship-building help Beltrán get a managerial job with the Mets or elsewhere? Lindor was asked and the shortstop is convinced the Hall of Famer will succeed in that realm if that's his desire.
"If he wants it. I believe he'll succeed whenever he becomes a manager," Lindor said. "If the organization feels that's the right fit for us…. If he decides to pursue, and if they feel he's the best fit, he'll succeed at it.
"To be a manager is not about respect, it's about knowing the game, making the right moves at the right time and connecting with players. And I think he can do all those."
"I love Francisco. I admire him. I love the way he plays. Being a switch-hitter, I'm always watching the switch-hitters in the game. He will be in this position at some point in life."
- Carlos Beltrán on Francisco Lindor pic.twitter.com/gwQGCW2KP5

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Juan Soto hit a three-run homer and the New York Mets kept the Philadelphia Phillies from gaining ground in the National League wild-card race with a 6-3 victory Friday night.
Edmundo Sosa went 3 for 3 with a home run and a double for the Phillies (85-69), who remained tied with the Cubs for the top two wild-card spots after Chicago lost 6-4 to Cincinnati. Both teams began the day one game ahead of the San Diego Padres, who were scheduled to host Miami later Friday.
Derek Hill also went deep and Bryson Stott had an RBI double for Philadelphia.
Soto also doubled and finished with three hits. A.J. Ewing’s two-run single capped a three-run first inning for the last-place Mets, who ended a five-game losing streak — their longest under interim manager Andy Green. Carson Benge had an RBI single in the first and reached base three times.
Francisco Lindor remained at 299 career homers after going 2 for 5 with a double.
Rookie left-hander Zac Thornton (5-5) allowed two runs and five hits in six innings. He struck out four and walked one. Thornton has permitted two runs or fewer eight times in 14 big league starts.
Dedniel Núñez got four outs for his second career save and first since July 13, 2024.
José Urquidy tossed 4 2/3 innings of scoreless bulk relief in his Phillies debut. Urquidy, designated for assignment by the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday, was claimed off waivers Thursday.
Phillies opener Tim Mayza (3-4) was charged with three runs. He threw 33 pitches but recorded just one out — the shortest outing by a Philadelphia starter since Cristopher Sánchez got only one out against the Washington Nationals on July 29, 2021.
Up next
The Mets will retire the No. 15 jersey worn by Hall of Fame center fielder Carlos Beltrán on Saturday before RHP Christian Scott (4-5, 3.76 ERA) opposes Phillies RHP Andrew Painter (3-9, 5.54).

item.content:encoded:
The Mets (70-84) defeated the Philadelphia Phillies (85-69) by a score of 6-3.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Mets left-handed starter Zac Thornton plunked leadoff batter Kyle Schwarber on a 3-2 count to get the game started. The rookie battled back, striking out Trea Turner and Bryce Harper before Mets first baseman Brett Baty made a diving stop on a Luis Arraez grounder down the line to put away the third out.
-- Southpaw Tim Mayza served as the bullpen opener for Philadelphia, and Francisco Lindor jumped all over him with a leadoff double. With one out, Bo Bichette worked a 10-pitch at-bat, culminating in a single to center field which moved Lindor up to third base. Carson Benge kept the line moving and drove in Lindor with an opposite-field single. Mark Vientos was walked to load the bases, and Phillies manager Don Mattingly pulled Mayza for right-handed reliever Jose Urquidy. A.J. Ewing roped an Urquidy fastball for a double, which scored two runs. Urquidy retired the next two Mets batters to limit the damage to three runs.
-- In the second inning, Ewing got turned around on a deep line drive to center, failing to haul in the RBI double for Bryson Stott, which cut the Mets' lead to 3-1. In the bottom half of the inning, Juan Soto doubled into the left-center field gap with two outs, but Urquidy struck out Bichette to end the threat.
-- With two outs away in the top of the sixth, Phillies left fielder Edmundo Sosa blasted a solo shot to left field, his third hit of the night. Excluding Sosa, Thornton allowed just two hits. He struck out four and walked one, allowing two earned runs across 87 pitches.
-- Soto took a hanging breaking ball thrown by Phillies right-hander Orion Kerkering 428 feet for a two-out three-run homer in the bottom of the sixth. Soto's 26th tater of 2026 put the Mets up 6-2.
-- Philadelphia center fielder Derek Hill responded with a solo home run off of Mets left-handed reliever Nate Lavender in the top of the seventh. Lavender persevered, retiring each of the next four batters he faced, before handing the ball to Dedniel Núñez to record the third out of the eighth. In the bottom half of the frame, Bichette grounded into a double play with the bases loaded. Núñez handled the ninth inning and retired the side to earn the first save of his season - and second save of his career - to seal the 6-3 win for the Mets.
Game MVP: Juan Soto
Soto notched his third game with multiple extra-base hits in September, going 3-for-5 with a double and a three-run homer. It was also Soto's third game of the season with at least three hits.
Highlights
What's next
The Mets play the Phillies in the third game of the four-game home series on Saturday at 4:10 p.m. on SNY. They will honor 2026 Baseball Hall of Fame inductee Carlos Beltrán.
New York will send out Christian Scott (3.76 ERA, 1.26 WHIP in 105.1 IP).
Philadelphia is set to start fellow right-hander Andrew Painter (5.54 ERA, 1.44 WHIP in 115.1 IP).
